props.title: Laws of Gravity
props.initialSlug: Two Brooklyn friends spiral into dangerous crime

sections.content: Laws of Gravity epitomizes the gritty independent film movement of early 1990s New York, landing somewhere between Martin Scorsese's Mean Streets (1973) and Nick Gomez's raw documentary style. Shot for just $38,000 on 16mm film, it follows small-time criminals Jimmy and Jon through Brooklyn's mean streets, capturing a visceral authenticity that influenced later works like The Yards (2000) and Little Odessa (1994). Peter Greene's explosive performance as Jimmy set a new standard for depicting volatile street criminals, predating similar characterizations in Pulp Fiction (1994).

sections.content: The film's handheld camerawork and use of actual locations established a template for 1990s independent crime dramas. Director Nick Gomez learned his craft working under Spike Lee, and that influence shows in the way he captures Brooklyn's texture and energy. The raw style influenced later works like Fresh (1994) and Clockers (1995), while also connecting back to predecessors like The Friends of Eddie Coyle (1973).

What sets Laws of Gravity apart is its unflinching portrayal of criminal life's mundane reality - the petty arguments, aimless hanging out, and sudden violence that defined certain corners of early 1990s Brooklyn. This approach influenced films like Night and the City (1992) and Federal Hill (1994), establishing a grittier alternative to the more stylized crime films of the era. sections.content: The success of Laws of Gravity helped pave the way for a wave of ultra-realistic crime dramas like Bound by Honor (1993) and New Jersey Drive (1995). Its influence can be seen in everything from the dialogue style to the documentary-like approach to violence, establishing a counterpoint to the more polished indie productions of the era like Reservoir Dogs (1992).
